entities.name: Vine
entities.tagline: Six seconds of looping infinite creativity.
entities.description: Vine was an American short-form video hosting service founded in June 2012 by Dom Hofmann, Rus Yusupov, and Colin Kroll. Acquired by Twitter in October 2012 before its official launch, Vine allowed users to record and share six-second looping video clips. It spawned a vibrant subculture of internet comedians, musicians, and creators before struggling with creator monetization, executive leadership churn, and fierce competition from Instagram.
entities.status_reason: Discontinued by parent company Twitter due to lack of monetization, creator defections to YouTube/Instagram, and product stagnation.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Acquired by Twitter prior to launch; failed to implement revenue sharing for top stars who migrated to YouTube and Instagram; Twitter shut down the upload network during company-wide cost-cutting.
entities.popularity_peak: 200M+ active viewers; 1.5B loop impressions/day

website.state_desc: Redirects to Twitter/X help center or archived portal; no loop player accessible.

app.store_status: Delisted from Apple App Store & Google Play
app.state_desc: Rebranded temporarily as 'Vine Camera' before being completely pulled.

api.state_desc: Underlying Vine endpoints and video CDN clusters were decommissioned.

community.state_desc: r/vine remains archived as a nostalgic memorial; creators shifted to TikTok.

domain.state_desc: Active DNS pointing to static archive landing.

entities.final_moments: On October 27, 2016, Twitter announced it would be discontinuing the Vine mobile app. Users were given a brief grace period to download their archives. On January 17, 2017, the original network was permanently shuttered, transitioning into a standalone camera app before fading into digital folklore.

entities.name: Google Reader
entities.tagline: The beating heart of the open, independent RSS web.
entities.description: Google Reader was a web-based aggregator capable of reading Atom and RSS feeds online or offline. Launched by Google engineer Chris Wetherell in 2005 through Google Labs, it became the undisputed central nervous system of internet publishing, journalism, and personal blog curation before Google abruptly announced its termination in 2013 to refocus on Google+.
entities.status_reason: Killed in Google's Spring Cleaning initiative in 2013 as part of a company push toward Google+.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Google decided RSS curation did not align with its algorithmic engagement goals; prioritized Google+ social integration; shut down despite fierce protests and petitions.
entities.popularity_peak: Tens of millions of daily power readers; backbone of tech journalism

website.state_desc: URL redirects to Google support sunset page.

api.state_desc: API completely shut down; caused numerous third-party apps like Reeder to break.

community.state_desc: Mass migration of power users to Feedly, Inoreader, and NewsBlur.

entities.final_moments: On March 13, 2013, Google posted 'A second spring of cleaning' on its official blog, announcing Reader would shut down on July 1. A public petition gathered over 150,000 signatures in days, but Google refused to budge. At midnight UTC on July 1, the servers ceased accepting feed syncs.

entities.name: GeoCities
entities.tagline: The original homestead of the weird, personal World Wide Web.
entities.description: GeoCities was a web hosting service founded in November 1994 by David Bohnett and John Rezner. Users selected a 'neighborhood' based on their topic (e.g., Hollywood for film, SiliconValley for tech, Area51 for sci-fi) and received free web space. It became the third-most visited website on Earth before being acquired by Yahoo in 1999 for $3.57 billion and eventually neglected to death.
entities.status_reason: Yahoo shut down GeoCities in the US on October 26, 2009, wiping millions of unique personal web pages.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Acquired by Yahoo during the dot-com bubble; suffered from lack of product vision, rise of modern social media (MySpace, Facebook), and Yahoo server cost cuts.
entities.popularity_peak: 3rd most visited website in the world (1999); 38M+ user pages

website.state_desc: Redirects to Yahoo Small Business / web hosting.

api.state_desc: HTML and FTP based; no API.

community.state_desc: Archive Team managed to scrape 1 Terabyte of pages right before Yahoo pulled the plug; inspired Neocities.

entities.final_moments: On April 23, 2009, Yahoo announced it would shutter GeoCities later that year. On October 26, 2009, Yahoo pulled the plug, deleting millions of user websites overnight. Jason Scott and the Archive Team mounted a heroic last-minute scraping mission to preserve whatever they could on BitTorrent.

entities.name: MSN Messenger
entities.tagline: The soundtrack of after-school dial-up connections and nudges.
entities.description: MSN Messenger (later rebranded Windows Live Messenger) was an instant messaging client created by Microsoft in 1999. It became the dominant communication channel for global teens throughout the 2000s, pioneering nudges, custom animated emoticons, status songs with Windows Media Player, and webcam video calls before being killed in favor of Skype.
entities.status_reason: Phased out globally in 2013 and China in 2014 following Microsoft's $8.5B acquisition of Skype.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Microsoft acquired Skype in 2011 for $8.5 billion and migrated all MSN user accounts into Skype, dismantling the MSN Messenger protocol servers.
entities.popularity_peak: 330M active monthly users (2009)

app.state_desc: Desktop client blocked by Microsoft auth servers; patched only by fan reverse-engineering (Escargot).

community.state_desc: Nostalgic developers created private server reimplementations like Escargot.

entities.final_moments: In November 2012, Microsoft announced plans to merge Windows Live Messenger into Skype. The rollout began in April 2013 across North America and Europe, with the final server in mainland China permanently unplugged on October 31, 2014.

entities.name: Adobe Flash
entities.tagline: The wild, interactive canvas that powered two decades of web creativity.
entities.description: Adobe Flash (originally FutureSplash Animator, then Macromedia Flash) was a multimedia software platform used for production of animations, rich web applications, desktop applications, mobile apps, and browser games. It allowed an entire generation of indie animators and developers to build games like Alien Hominid, FarmVille, and Homestar Runner before open web standards (HTML5, WebGL) and Apple's refusal to support it on iOS sealed its demise.
entities.status_reason: Officially sunset by Adobe on December 31, 2020; blocked from running in all modern web browsers on January 12, 2021.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Notorious security exploits, extreme battery consumption on mobile devices, Steve Jobs' famous 2010 'Thoughts on Flash' memo, and the rise of native HTML5/CSS3/JavaScript rendering.
entities.popularity_peak: Installed on over 98% of internet-connected desktop computers (2005)

app.state_desc: Never allowed on iOS; killed on Android in 2012.

community.state_desc: Preserved by open-source Rust emulator Ruffle and BlueMaxima's Flashpoint archive project.

entities.final_moments: In July 2017, Adobe partnered with Apple, Google, Microsoft, and Mozilla to announce that Flash Player would be retired at the end of 2020. Adobe embedded a logic bomb in version 32.0.0.371 that stopped Flash Player from loading SWF content after January 12, 2021.

entities.name: Napster (Original)
entities.tagline: The P2P earthquake that tore the music industry wide open.
entities.description: Napster was a pioneering peer-to-peer file sharing Internet service created in 1999 by Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker. It focused on sharing digital audio files, primarily MP3s. At its peak, 80 million registered users traded billions of songs without copyright authorization, triggering historic lawsuits from Metallica, Dr. Dre, and the RIAA that eventually crushed the original architecture in federal court.
entities.status_reason: The original revolutionary P2P decentralized protocol died in 2001. The trademark was auctioned, sold to Roxio, Best Buy, Rhapsody, and now exists as a generic paid streaming zombie.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Shut down following landmark federal copyright infringement injunctions (A&M Records, Inc. v. Napster, Inc.); filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2002; assets liquidated.
entities.popularity_peak: 80 million registered users; over 2 billion songs downloaded

website.state_desc: Operates as a generic corporate music streaming platform owned by Hivemind and Algorand.

app.state_desc: App exists on iOS/Android, but has 0% relationship to the original decentralized MP3 network.

api.state_desc: Original central indexing servers permanently silenced in 2001.

community.state_desc: Paved the way for Limewire, Kazaa, BitTorrent, the iTunes Store, and Spotify.

domain.state_desc: Domain passed through 5 corporate owners since bankruptcy auction.

entities.final_moments: On March 5, 2001, Judge Marilyn Hall Patel issued a preliminary injunction ordering Napster to remove all copyrighted music listed by plaintiffs within 72 hours. On July 11, 2001, Napster shut down its entire network to comply with the order. It never reopened as a free service.

entities.description: Club Penguin was a massively multiplayer online game involving a virtual world that contained a range of online games and activities. Created by New Horizon Interactive in 2005, players used cartoon penguin-avatars and lived in a snow-covered virtual world. Acquired by Disney in 2007 for $350 million, it became a cultural milestone for Millennial and Gen Z childhoods before being shut down in 2017 to promote mobile app Club Penguin Island.
entities.status_reason: Disney shut down Club Penguin desktop servers on March 29, 2017; mobile successor Club Penguin Island also died in 2018.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Flash deprecation, declining desktop web traffic, Disney refocusing on mobile app 'Club Penguin Island' (which failed and shut down a year later).

entities.name: Google Wave
entities.tagline: The real-time collaboration miracle that arrived a decade too early.
entities.description: Google Wave was a dynamic personal communication and collaborative web tool announced by Google at Google I/O on May 27, 2009. Developed by the Rasmussen brothers (creators of Google Maps), it merged email, instant messaging, wiki, and document editing into a single live stream with real-time character-by-character typing and playback. It overwhelmed users with complexity and was abandoned by Google in 2010.
entities.status_reason: Google ceased development in August 2010 due to low adoption, handing the code to the Apache Software Foundation before complete retirement in 2012.
entities.cause_of_death_summary: Extreme product complexity, slow web performance in 2009 browsers, lack of clear enterprise use cases, and invite-only exclusivity that killed initial viral momentum.

Crucial components of its operational transformation technology were subsequently extracted and integrated into Google Docs.

entities.description: Pebble was a smartwatch developed by Pebble Technology Corporation, founded by Eric Migicovsky. Funded via a record-breaking $10.2 million Kickstarter campaign in 2012, Pebble featured an always-on memory LCD e-paper display, tactile physical buttons, 7-day battery life, and an open SDK for developers. It was acquired by Fitbit in December 2016 and shut down, though its loyal community resurrected it as Rebble.

entities.cause_of_death_summary: Cash-flow crisis, declining consumer hardware margins, aggressive competition from Apple Watch, and failed debt renegotiation; sold to Fitbit for just $23M.

entities.tagline: The pioneer lifecaster with a webcam strapped to his baseball cap that gave birth to Twitch.
entities.description: Justin.tv was launched on March 19, 2007, by Justin Kan, Emmett Shear, Michael Seibel, and Kyle Vogt. entities.name: Dailybooth
entities.tagline: The daily selfie photo community that captured the internet's face before Instagram existed.
entities.description: Dailybooth was founded in February 2009 by Jon Wheatley and Ryan Freitas with the motto 'Your life in pictures.' Users took a webcam photo every day accompanied by a short caption, building a visual time-lapse of their lives and spawning YouTube vlogger micro-celebrities. Gaining 3 million photos in its first year, it was eclipsed when smartphones with front-facing cameras and Instagram arrived. Acquired by Airbnb in August 2012, Dailybooth shut down on November 14, 2012.

entities.popularity_peak: Over 10 million photos uploaded; the defining community of early YouTube creators in 2009-2010
